Privacy policy

Effective 2026-09-22

The short version

ArcPace has no accounts, no analytics, no ads, no tracking and no server of its own. Everything it knows about you lives on your device, and I never see it.

Two things do leave your phone, because they have to: your location goes to a weather service so it can fetch a forecast, and a city name you type goes to a geocoding service so it can be found on a map. Neither is tied to your name or to any identifier for you, because ArcPace does not have one.

Who this covers

ArcPace is made and published by one person, Stephen Chou, from a personal developer account. There is no company behind it. Where this policy says "I", that is who it means.

It covers the ArcPace app for iPhone. It applies from the date at the top and replaces any earlier version.

What ArcPace stores on your device

All of it stays in the app's own storage on your device. It is not sent to me and I cannot read it.

  • Your preferences: easy pace, run distance, the hours you can run, heat and cold tolerance, units and appearance.
  • The place you last looked at, any cities you saved, and a copy of the most recent forecast so the app opens instantly.
  • If you add the ArcPace widget: the next day of hourly scores for your current place, kept where the widget can read them. The widget shows your city and the weather on your Home Screen or Lock Screen, where anyone holding your phone can see it.
  • If you allow Health access: a summary of each running workout from the last sixteen weeks — when it happened, how long and far it was, average heart rate if your device recorded one, and, where a GPS route exists, where it went. ArcPace uses the route only to work out where the run happened.
  • Where you told ArcPace a run happened, if the workout had no route of its own.
  • The fact that you tipped, so the thank-you reads correctly. Not the amount, and nothing about how you paid.
  • The day you first opened ArcPace, which days you have opened it since (the last thirty), and when it last asked you for an App Store rating — so it asks rarely, and never in your first two weeks.

Location

ArcPace asks for your location only while you are using it, and uses it for one thing: fetching the forecast for where you are. It never tracks you in the background and does not record where you have been.

To fetch a forecast, your coordinates are sent to Apple Weather. If Apple Weather cannot answer, they are sent to Open-Meteo as a backup, and the app says so. The provider receives the coordinates and the request, and nothing else — no name, no email, no account, because ArcPace has none of those.

To turn coordinates into a city name, ArcPace uses Apple's built-in location services. When you search for a city by name, the text you type is sent to Open-Meteo's geocoding service.

You can decline location access and search for a place by name instead. You can change your mind at any time in Settings → Privacy & Security → Location Services.

Health data

If you allow it, ArcPace reads your running workouts from Apple Health so it can show how the weather affected your past runs and tune its score to you. Reading is all it does: it never writes to Health, and it reads only workouts, distance, heart rate, running speed and workout routes.

Your health data stays on your device. ArcPace never uploads it, never shares it with anyone, never sells it, and never uses it for advertising or marketing of any kind. I do not have a server it could go to.

One thing to know: to score a past run, ArcPace looks up what the weather was at that place and hour. That lookup sends the approximate location and time of the run to Apple Weather — the same kind of request as a forecast. It does not send the workout, your heart rate, your pace, or anything that identifies you.

You can revoke access at any time in the Health app under Sharing → Apps and Services → ArcPace. ArcPace keeps working; the History tab simply goes empty.

This section also serves as the consumer health data notice that some U.S. states require. The categories collected are listed above; the purpose is to show and score your own runs to you; the source is Apple Health on your device; no category is shared with or sold to anyone; and the way to exercise your rights over it is to revoke access in Health or delete the app, either of which removes it.

Sharing a run

On a past run you can make a picture of what the weather did to it and share it through the iPhone share sheet. The picture holds only what you see on it before you share: the date, the score, the pace the weather cost, what the run was worth on an ordinary day (a pace, adjusted for the weather), the conditions, and the place name unless you switch it off. Nothing else about the run goes with it.

If the run has a GPS route, ArcPace asks Apple's location services for the name of the town it was in, so it can offer that name for the picture. That sends the run's location, rounded to about a kilometre, to Apple — the same kind of request as naming your current location — and nothing else about the run.

ArcPace makes the picture on your device and hands it to the app you choose. It is not sent to me or anywhere else unless you send it. What happens to it after that is up to you and that app.

Tips

Tips are in-app purchases handled entirely by Apple. Apple takes the payment under its own privacy policy and terms; I never see your card, your name or your Apple ID. ArcPace learns only that a purchase completed.

What ArcPace does not do

  • No analytics or usage tracking of any kind — I do not know how many people use it or what they tap.
  • No advertising, and no advertising identifiers.
  • No crash reporting service.
  • No accounts, sign-in, email address or phone number.
  • No selling, renting or sharing of anything, with anyone, ever.

Backups

Because ArcPace's data lives in ordinary app storage, it is included in your device backup — iCloud Backup or a backup to your computer — if you have those turned on. That copy is governed by Apple's terms and your own backup settings, not by ArcPace.

Children

ArcPace is not directed at children under 13, and I do not knowingly collect anything from anyone — of any age. If a child has used it, deleting the app removes everything.

Your rights

Most privacy laws give you the right to see, correct, export and delete the personal data an organisation holds about you. I hold none, so there is nothing for me to show you or delete. Every right you have is exercised on your own device:

  • To see it: it is what the app shows you.
  • To delete it: delete the app. iOS removes everything ArcPace stored.
  • To stop location access: Settings → Privacy & Security → Location Services → ArcPace.
  • To stop Health access: Health app → Sharing → Apps and Services → ArcPace.
  • For data the weather providers or Apple hold, their policies linked above explain your rights with them.

Changes

If a future version of ArcPace changes what leaves your device, this policy will change with it and the date at the top will move. The current version is always in the app under Settings, and at the address below.

Contact

Questions about privacy: arcpace.app@gmail.com. I am one person, so give me a few days.

If you email me, including through Send feedback in Settings, I see your address and what you write, and use them only to reply. The app attaches nothing to the message.

Terms of use

Effective 2026-09-22

The short version

ArcPace is a forecast and a model. It tells you what the weather is likely to cost you on a run. It is not a doctor, a coach or a guarantee, and the decision to run — and to stop — is always yours.

Agreement

These terms are between you and Stephen Chou, the individual who makes and publishes ArcPace. By installing or using ArcPace, you agree to them. If you do not, please do not use it.

Your licence to use the app is Apple's standard Licensed Application End User Licence Agreement. These terms add to it. Where the two conflict, Apple's agreement wins.

Apple Licensed Application EULA ↗

Not medical advice

ArcPace gives general guidance for healthy adults. Nothing in it is medical advice, and it does not know your health, your medication, your acclimatisation or how you feel today. A score, a pace penalty, a heat-stress flag, a "what to bring" list or a "best time to run" is an estimate from a weather model, not a clearance to go.

Heat illness is serious and comes on fast. ArcPace flags forecast thunderstorms and freezing rain when its weather provider reports them, and a forecast can miss both. Cold, lightning, air quality, traffic, terrain, darkness and your own condition are all outside what ArcPace measures or guarantees. If you feel dizzy, stop sweating, feel confused or unwell: stop running and get help, whatever the app says.

If you have a medical condition, are pregnant, are new to running or are returning from illness or injury, talk to a doctor before relying on any running guidance, including this one.

Forecasts are forecasts

Weather data comes from third parties — Apple Weather, with Open-Meteo as a backup — and is passed on as I receive it. Forecasts are wrong sometimes, sometimes badly; conditions on a specific street can differ from the model; and a provider can be down. ArcPace clamps readings to physical limits and tells you when data is missing, but it cannot make a forecast true.

Past-run scoring uses historical weather for roughly where and when a run happened. Where a run has no GPS route, the location is one you supplied or a default, and the score is marked approximate. Treat it that way.

Weather data from Apple is provided under Apple's attribution and terms; Open-Meteo data is licensed CC BY 4.0. Both are credited in the app.

Your health data

If you allow Health access, ArcPace reads your workouts to score them. How complete and accurate that data is depends on the watch or app that recorded it, and many devices write less to Apple Health than they show in their own apps. ArcPace can only work with what is there.

You are responsible for the permissions you grant. The Privacy Policy describes exactly what is read and where it stays.

Tips

ArcPace is free and complete without tipping. Tips are voluntary, one-off, and unlock nothing — no feature is held back from anyone who does not tip.

A tip is an in-app purchase processed by Apple, subject to Apple's terms and refund policy; I cannot issue refunds directly.

Using ArcPace

You may use ArcPace for your own personal, non-commercial running. You may not copy, sell, rent, reverse-engineer or redistribute it, remove its credits, or use it in a way that breaks the law or the terms of the app store you got it from. You may not use it to make automated requests to the weather providers.

ArcPace and its design, code and text are mine. Weather data belongs to its providers. Your data is yours.

No warranty

ArcPace is provided "as is" and "as available", without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including any warranty of accuracy, fitness for a particular purpose, merchantability or non-infringement, to the fullest extent the law allows. I do not promise it will be uninterrupted, error-free, or right.

Limitation of liability

To the fullest extent the law allows, I am not liable for any indirect, incidental, special, consequential or punitive damages, or for any injury, loss or damage arising from your use of ArcPace or reliance on anything it shows — including decisions about whether, when, where or how to run. Where liability cannot be excluded, it is limited to the greater of the total you paid me in tips in the twelve months before the claim and ten US dollars.

Some jurisdictions do not allow some of these limits. Where that applies to you, they apply only as far as the law permits.

Indemnity

If a third party brings a claim against me because of something you did with ArcPace in breach of these terms, you agree to cover the reasonable costs of dealing with it.

Changes and ending

I may change ArcPace or these terms. The current terms are always in the app under Settings, with the date they took effect. Continuing to use ArcPace after a change means you accept it. You can stop at any time by deleting the app. I may stop distributing ArcPace, or stop a version working, at any time.

Law and disputes

These terms are governed by the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia, United States, without regard to conflict-of-law rules, and any dispute will be brought in the courts there — unless the law where you live gives you a right to something else, in which case that right stands. If any part of these terms is found unenforceable, the rest still applies.
